title: Revamping Europe's chips strategy: indispensability, not self-sufficiency
method: structured qualitative stock-take of the Chips Act's implementation using state-aid approval totals, ECA findings and case evidence (Intel Magdeburg cancellation, Nexperia), with comparison to US CHIPS Act awards
outcomes: state aid mobilised under Pillar II, strategic coordination, flagship fab investments, fit with European chip demand
headline: Only EUR 13.75 billion of state aid had been approved under the Chips Act, against USD 33.7 billion in grants and USD 5.5 billion in loans awarded under the US CHIPS Act by January 2025; the authors judge the Act has 'underdelivered' on funding scale and coordination.
summary_plain: Bruegel looked back at what the EU Chips Act has achieved since 2023. It finds far less public money has flowed than planned, the flagship Intel factory in Germany was cancelled, and the subsidies do not match what European chip buyers (mainly carmakers and industry) actually need.
quality: Descriptive stock-take relying largely on secondary data (ECA, state-aid decisions); no counterfactual; written as input to the Chips Act 2 revision.
interested_party: Bruegel is funded partly by EU member states and corporate members, including technology firms

title: Annual Report on the Strategic Technologies for Europe Platform (STEP) 2024 (COM(2025) 322 final)
venue: Report from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council
method: descriptive statistics from programme monitoring data (calls, earmarked budgets, cohesion programme amendments, STEP Seals awarded) for STEP's first year
outcomes: EU funding aligned to STEP, cohesion-policy reprogramming, STEP Seals, RRF uptake
headline: In 2024 over EUR 10 billion of EU funds were aligned with STEP (EUR 4.6 billion under direct management and EUR 5.9 billion in 29 approved cohesion-programme amendments), 162 STEP Seals were awarded across 23 Member States, and no Member State amended its Recovery and Resilience Plan to use STEP.
summary_plain: STEP does not have its own budget; it redirects money from existing EU programmes towards strategic technologies. In its first year about EUR 10 billion was steered this way, mostly towards clean technologies, but countries did not use the option to redirect recovery-fund money.
quality: Official first-year monitoring; inputs and outputs only (money earmarked, labels awarded), no outcome or impact measurement; self-reported by the Commission.
interested_party: European Commission reporting on its own programme

authors: Paul Simmonds; Kleitia Zeqo; Matthias Ploeg; Alexandre Lotito; Ivette Oomens; Sophie Viscido; Emma Coroler; Jonathan Puerta; Tomas van den Broeke (Technopolis Group)
title: Interim Evaluation of the Digital Europe Programme: Final report (supporting study)
venue: Publications Office of the EU (study for DG CNECT), doi:10.2759/8693841
method: mixed-methods programme evaluation: public consultation, surveys of beneficiaries, applicants and end users, stakeholder interviews, three case studies, monitoring-indicator analysis; plus JRC RHOMOLO model projections (ex-ante component)
outcomes: progress on programme indicators, end-user reach, beneficiary-reported benefits, efficiency, coherence
headline: The programme had engaged over 55,000 SMEs as end users by end-2024, which the study notes is only about 0.2% of the EU's almost 26 million SMEs; 55% of beneficiaries reported stronger cross-border networks and 36% an improved ability to deliver new products and services.
summary_plain: Consultants hired by the Commission reviewed how the EU's Digital Europe funding programme performed up to 2024. It has built major infrastructure (supercomputers, AI test facilities, digital innovation hubs) and participants report benefits, but its direct reach to businesses is still small and red tape and low awareness remain problems.
period_geography: EU-27 plus associated countries, 2021 to end-2024
quality: Contractor study behind the Commission's SWD(2025) 420 (already listed); survey-based self-reported benefits, no counterfactual; GDP effects are model projections, not observed.
interested_party: Commissioned and paid for by the European Commission (DG CNECT), which runs the programme

authors: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (Carpentier, D'Adda, Nepelski, Stake)
title: European Digital Innovation Hubs Network's activities and customers: State of Play 2024 (JRC140547)
method: descriptive monitoring statistics on EDIH services plus before/after comparison of Digital Maturity Assessment Tool scores for about 9,000-10,000 SMEs and 800 public organisations
outcomes: services delivered, events, regional coverage, change in customers' digital maturity scores
headline: By September 2024 EDIHs had organised over 5,000 events reaching more than 200,000 participants and delivered over 18,000 services; 90% of assessed users improved their digital maturity score, with AI and automation scores rising by up to 35%.
summary_plain: The EU funds a network of local digital innovation hubs that help small firms and public bodies go digital. The Commission's research centre found that nine in ten organisations that were assessed twice scored higher on digital maturity after getting help.
quality: Before/after scores with no control group and self-assessed tool, so gains cannot be attributed to the hubs; the Commission's own research service evaluating a Commission programme. Report PDF not accessible from here; findings read from JRC and EDIH official landing pages.
interested_party: European Commission (JRC) assessing a Commission-funded network

authors: Elodie Carpentier; Diego D'Adda; Daniel Nepelski
title: Which firms receive digital innovation support? Evidence from the European Digital Innovation Hubs network
venue: International Small Business Journal: Researching Entrepreneurship
method: comparison of about 15,600 EDIH customer firms with the broader European business population (firm-level demographics, performance, capital structure, innovativeness)
headline: Comparing about 15,600 EDIH customer firms with the wider business population, EDIH customers are larger, faster-growing and more concentrated in high-tech, knowledge-intensive and ICT sectors, suggesting less digitally advanced firms may be systematically underserved.
summary_plain: Researchers checked which companies actually use the EU-funded digital innovation hubs. They found the hubs mostly help firms that are already bigger, growing and tech-savvy, rather than the laggards the programme most wants to reach.
quality: Large firm-level dataset; descriptive comparison of selection, not an impact estimate; authors are JRC staff (Commission).
interested_party: Authors work at the European Commission's JRC

authors: Dorota Czyżewska-Misztal; Sébastien Bourdin; Fabien Nadou; Piotr Idczak
title: Digital innovation hubs as territorial intermediaries: Aligning European digital strategy with local needs
method: qualitative study based on 43 in-depth interviews with DIH/EDIH representatives, Commission stakeholders and network coordinators
outcomes: implementation of EDIH policy at regional level, roles of hubs, policy-local mismatches
headline: Based on 43 interviews, the hubs act as promoters, facilitators and enablers of SME digitalisation, but there are persistent mismatches between EU policy objectives and local implementation, especially in less digitally advanced regions.
summary_plain: Interviews with people running and overseeing EU digital innovation hubs show the hubs adapt to local needs, but EU goals and what happens on the ground often do not line up, particularly in regions that are already behind digitally.
quality: Qualitative interview evidence, no quantified outcomes; covers DIHs broadly, not only DEP-funded EDIHs. First names of some authors taken from Crossref record.

authors: European Cybersecurity Industrial, Technology and Research Competence Centre (ECCC)
title: Consolidated Annual Activity Report 2025 (Governing Board Decision No 2026/4)
method: descriptive statistics from the body's own monitoring (calls, proposals, grants, project portfolio, staffing, NCC network activity) plus a community needs survey (350 responses)
outcomes: call and grant throughput, project portfolio, NCC network operation, awareness among the cybersecurity community
headline: In its first year as an autonomous body the ECCC ran 165 ongoing Digital Europe projects by December 2025 (e.g. 32 of 172 proposals funded under a EUR 102.8 million deployment call); a 350-response community survey found 85% of respondents not fully aware of the National Coordination Centres' tasks.
summary_plain: The EU's cybersecurity funding centre in Bucharest reports on its 2025 work: it is now running on its own, handles about 165 funded projects, and is building a network of national centres, but most people in the sector it surveyed do not know well what those national centres do.
quality: Self-reported activity report; inputs and outputs only, no impact measurement; survey results are preliminary.
interested_party: The ECCC reporting on its own activity

title: EUrope's digital transition: Assessing the effectiveness of the 2030 Digital Decade Policy Programme
venue: REGROUP Focus Paper No. 2 (European Policy Centre; republished by CIDOB)
method: desk review of the 2023 and 2024 State of the Digital Decade reports and national roadmaps, with country cases (Finland, Belgium, Italy, Bulgaria) and expert discussions
outcomes: progress towards Digital Decade targets (skills, connectivity, business digitalisation, public services), funding, coherence
headline: Drawing on the Commission's own projections, the EU is off track on all Digital Decade targets: only 59% of people are projected to have basic digital skills by 2030 against an 80% target, and about 12 million ICT specialists against a 20 million goal.
summary_plain: A Brussels think tank reviewed how the EU is doing against its 2030 digital goals. Using official progress reports, it concludes Europe is behind on every target and calls for more realistic goals, better funding and stronger accountability.
quality: Secondary analysis of Commission monitoring data plus expert discussions; no new data or causal design.
interested_party: Funded under the EU's Horizon Europe programme (REGROUP project)

title: The use of corporate mobility instruments and Brexit: An empirical analysis
method: descriptive analysis of a hand-collected dataset of cross-border mergers and SE seat transfers out of the UK, 1 January 2017 to 30 November 2019
outcomes: use of cross-border merger (Directive 2017/1132 Title II Ch. II) and SE seat-transfer instruments to relocate from the UK
headline: Between January 2017 and November 2019, UK companies used cross-border mergers and SE seat transfers to move to other EU Member States, mainly in the financial sector but also in other sectors.
summary_plain: Before Brexit, some UK companies used the EU's company-law tools for cross-border mergers to move into the EU. Most were financial firms, showing these legal routes were actually used when firms needed them.
quality: Descriptive counts of instrument use, no counterfactual; concerns the cross-border merger rules codified in Directive 2017/1132. Abstract gives no counts. Same authors as the listed 2019 report but a separate article.
